Microsoft is rolling out Linux container support to WSL — May Read

Microsoft has made WSL Containers generally available, adding a native Windows CLI and API for building and running Linux containers without relying on separate container tooling. The release adds enterprise controls through Defender for Endpoint and Intune, while Docker Compose-compatible support is planned.

  • Microsoft has made WSL Containers generally available, allowing users to build, run, and deploy Linux containers on Windows through the new wslc.exe command-line tool or its container.exe alias.
  • The general availability release adds container restart, file copy, health check, network connection management, real-time event, mount, and configurable storage-location capabilities.
  • WSL Containers integrates with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint so security teams can view container process, file, and network activity and connect it to the Windows host.
  • Microsoft Intune can disable WSL Containers or restrict developers to container images from administrator-approved registries.
  • Microsoft is developing Docker Compose-style support intended to allow wsl compose up to work with existing compose.yaml files unchanged.

Microsoft Breach by Midnight Blizzard (APT29): What Happened? — Should Read

Midnight Blizzard (APT29) reportedly used password spraying against a poorly secured Microsoft test tenant, then abused legacy OAuth app permissions and Entra ID roles to create persistent malicious applications with broad Exchange Online mailbox access. The incident highlights the need for MFA everywhere, strict least-privilege controls, and continuous auditing of app registrations, service principals, and consent grants.

  • The article attributes the Microsoft campaign to Midnight Blizzard, also known as APT29 or Cozy Bear, and describes the group as linked to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
  • The attackers obtained initial access by password spraying a non-production Microsoft test tenant that lacked multi-factor authentication.
  • The article says the attackers abused a legacy OAuth application and Microsoft Entra ID permissions to create a new user and assign high-privilege roles in Microsoft’s corporate tenant.
  • The attackers created malicious OAuth applications and granted them the Office 365 Exchange Online full_access_as_app permission, enabling access to corporate mailboxes.
  • The article recommends enforcing multi-factor authentication, auditing permissions and application registrations, monitoring unusual activity, and securing legacy and test systems.

Technologies: identity-provider, iam, cloud-platform, mfa

Products: microsoft-entra-id, microsoft-graph, exchange-online, office-365

Vendors: microsoft, mitiga

How Okta Passwords Can Be Compromised: Uncovering a Risk to User Data — Should Read

Okta audit logs can store passwords in plaintext when users mistakenly enter them in the username field during a failed login, exposing credentials to anyone with access to those logs or forwarded SIEM data. Organizations should identify and rotate affected credentials, restrict log access, and enforce phishing-resistant MFA.

  • Okta audit logs can record a password in plaintext when a user mistakenly enters it in the username field during a failed login attempt.
  • People who can read Okta audit logs, including through a SIEM system where those logs are forwarded, may be able to access exposed user passwords.
  • Mitiga reported identifying hundreds of potentially leaked passwords and credentials for customers, including administrator-level users, by matching failed and successful login events.
  • Multi-factor authentication can reduce the risk from exposed passwords, but the article notes that phishing, repeated approval requests, and session hijacking may still be used to bypass it.
  • Mitiga recommends identifying affected users with its query, rotating their passwords, limiting and monitoring access to logs, educating users, and enabling MFA.

US Air Force members given over 6 years in prison for cyber theft of more than $2 million — May Read

Two U.S. Air Force members received prison sentences of more than six and nine years for a business email compromise scheme that stole over $2 million by phishing credentials and diverting corporate wire payments.

  • U.S. Air Force members Chijioke Timothy Odimegwu and Harafat Mogaji were sentenced for a business email compromise scheme that stole more than $2 million from organizations.
  • The pair used phishing emails to obtain employee email credentials, then monitored payment discussions and sent altered wiring instructions to redirect funds into accounts they controlled.
  • Prosecutors said the scheme targeted at least 15 victim organizations and ran for more than two years while the men were stationed at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware.
  • Odimegwu received a prison sentence of more than nine years and was ordered to pay $366,617 in restitution, while Mogaji received 6.5 years and was ordered to pay $995,680.
  • Both men pleaded guilty in June to wire fraud, identity theft, and access-device fraud, and each will serve three years of supervised release after prison.

OpenAI pledged $1 billion in subsidized frontier-AI access and training through its Daybreak for Frontline Defenders program to help small security teams at essential-service providers identify vulnerabilities, detect suspicious activity, and respond to intrusions.

  • The program will help defenders search for critical software weaknesses, investigate suspicious activity in their technology systems, and stop harmful actions after hackers gain access.

New Spectre-v2 BTR Attack Leaks Linux Memory Despite Existing Defenses — Should Read

Researchers disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre-v2 technique that abuses stale branch-prediction entries in JIT engines to transiently execute reused code locations and leak secrets. Proof-of-concept Linux kernel exploits recovered a root password hash from fully patched Intel systems, and fixes have been merged for the affected cBPF JIT.

  • Researchers from VUSec and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre-v2 variant affecting JIT engines.
  • BTR exploits stale indirect branch-prediction entries that can remain after JIT-generated code is freed and its memory is reused, enabling transient control-flow hijacking and data disclosure.
  • The researchers found SpiderMonkey, GraalVM, and the Linux kernel's cBPF JIT affected, with differing exploitability and data-leakage rates.
  • Two proof-of-concept Linux kernel exploits recovered a root password hash within minutes from a fully patched Intel system with default protections enabled.
  • Linux mitigations for BTR were released and merged as CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508, while GraalVM randomized JIT code-cache locations and Mozilla is prioritizing site isolation.

Technologies: browser, operating-system

Products: firefox, spidermonkey, graalvm, linux-kernel, cbpf-jit

Vendors: vusec, scuola-superiore-santanna, mozilla, oracle, intel, amd, linux-kernel

Automated AI agent used to breach cybersecurity nonprofit DIVD — Should Read

Dutch vulnerability-disclosure nonprofit DIVD says it was breached through an undisclosed technical flaw, with an autonomous AI agent conducting noisy and poorly executed post-exploitation activity. The organization is investigating, has notified authorities, and plans to share more details on October 1.

  • The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) reported that it was breached through an undisclosed technical vulnerability that it said was not Citrix NetScaler.
  • DIVD said the intruder used an automated AI agent for post-compromise activity, with the agent choosing its next steps autonomously.
  • According to DIVD, the activity was loud and messy, and the agent made mistakes such as disrupting its own password-spraying attempt during an adversary-in-the-middle operation.
  • DIVD notified police, the Dutch data-protection authority, and the National Cyber Security Center, and said its investigation is ongoing.
  • DIVD plans to provide a more detailed update on October 1 and notify other possible victims of the same vulnerability when it can.

Microsoft has begun broadly rolling out Windows 11 26H2, a small enablement update for 24H2 and 25H2 systems that mainly resets the support lifecycle because most features have already arrived through monthly updates. PCs running the separate 26H1 branch cannot upgrade directly to 26H2.

  • Many 26H2 features may already be present on fully updated systems because Microsoft has been introducing them through monthly updates.
  • For commercial PCs, 26H2 enables Windows settings backup, app-specific taskbar actions, and some File Explorer improvements that were not previously enabled by default.
  • Devices running Windows 11 version 26H1 cannot update directly to 26H2 because 26H1 uses a different Windows core.

Here We Go Again (Citrix NetScaler DTLS Preauth Memory Overflow CVE-2026-88772) — Must Read

CVE-2026-88772 is an actively exploited, pre-authentication DTLS memory overflow in Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway VPN virtual servers with DTLS enabled by default, which can lead to remote code execution. Organizations should urgently upgrade to Citrix's fixed releases or disable DTLS where operationally feasible.

  • CVE-2026-88772 is a Citrix NetScaler DTLS memory overflow that can cause remote code execution or denial of service before authentication when DTLS is enabled.
  • Citrix reported CVE-2026-88772 as exploited in the wild, and DTLS is enabled by default on NetScaler VPN virtual servers unless an administrator turns it off.
  • The vulnerable NetScaler 14.1-73.30 code copies a reassembled chain of packet buffers into a fixed 35,840-byte scratch buffer without checking the total size.
  • The article demonstrates that 120 crafted DTLS records can cause approximately 173,665 bytes to be copied, overflowing the scratch buffer by 137,825 bytes.
  • Citrix recommends upgrading NetScaler ADC and Gateway to fixed releases including 14.1-73.37 or later and 13.1-64.23 or later.

Technologies: load-balancer, vpn, remote-access

Products: citrix-netscaler-adc, citrix-netscaler-gateway

Vendors: citrix, cloud-software-group

Building a certificate authority for the whole Internet — Should Read

Cloudflare plans to become a publicly trusted certificate authority, combining a newly applied-for root program presence with an acquired GlobalSign root to provide broadly compatible, automated TLS certificates. It also intends to support ACME-first issuance and post-quantum Merkle Tree Certificates beginning in early 2027.

  • Cloudflare announced its intent to become a publicly trusted certificate authority but stated that it is not issuing certificates yet.
  • Cloudflare has applied to the Chrome, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla root programs and signed a definitive agreement to acquire an established broadly trusted root from GlobalSign.
  • Cloudflare plans to offer automated certificate issuance and renewal through ACME, requiring customers to support ACME Renewal Information for issuance.
  • Cloudflare intends to publish reproducible builds of its certificate-signing software, attest the hardware security modules holding its keys, and operate a public dashboard for issuance health and incidents.
  • Cloudflare plans to issue production post-quantum Merkle Tree Certificates in the first quarter of 2027.

Russian pizza chain with 1,500 locations confirms cyberattack following hacker claims — Should Read

Dodo Pizza confirmed that hackers accessed customer personal and order data after DataSuckers claimed it stole records for 68 million customers, though the scope remains unverified. The company says payment data was not affected, attacker access has been blocked, and an investigation is underway.

  • Dodo Pizza confirmed that attackers accessed its systems and may have obtained customer names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and order details.
  • Dodo Pizza said it does not store customer payment information, so payment data was not compromised, and it has blocked the attackers’ access while investigating the incident.
  • DataSuckers claimed it stole records for 68 million customers across multiple countries and 15 years of order history, but those claims have not been independently verified.
  • DataSuckers said it planned to publish some of the alleged data and offered the database for sale for about $100,000.
  • Dodo Pizza said it notified Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, about the incident.

Arizona Supreme Court says hackers stole residents’ personal data — Should Read

The Arizona Supreme Court says criminal hackers copied personally identifiable information belonging to many Arizona residents from the state court system. The incident was not ransomware and no ransom demand has been reported; officials are notifying affected people and working with the FBI.

  • The Arizona Supreme Court said criminal hackers copied personally identifiable information about many Arizona residents from the state court system.
  • Arizona Supreme Court Chief Justice Ann Scott Timmer said the Administrative Office of the Courts is working to alert as many people as possible whose information it believes was copied.
  • A court-system spokesperson said the incident did not involve ransomware, and no ransom demand had been made as of Monday.
  • The court is withholding further details because releasing them could affect the investigation, and officials are working with the FBI.
  • No hacking group has publicly claimed responsibility for the incident.

Vietnamese man charged in $16 million 'pig butchering' crypto scam — Should Read

A Vietnamese national, Trung Nguyen Van, was charged in the U.S. with laundering cryptocurrency tied to pig-butchering scams, including about $16 million stolen from one victim. Authorities say his wallets received more than $53 million from fraud schemes targeting U.S. victims between 2018 and 2024.

  • Vietnamese national Trung Nguyen Van was charged with money laundering for his alleged role in a pig-butchering cryptocurrency scam that defrauded one victim of about $16 million.
  • The victim transferred cryptocurrency to Van's wallet between June and August 2024 while believing they were investing through a platform called Triangle.
  • Court documents state that Van's cryptocurrency wallets received approximately $53.3 million from wire fraud schemes targeting U.S. citizens between February 2018 and December 2024.
  • Authorities linked at least $24 million in crypto assets received by Van's wallets to known pig-butchering schemes.
  • The FBI reported that investment scams accounted for $8.6 billion in losses in 2025, or 49% of all scam-related incidents.

It Failed Three Auth Checks, Then Got Whitelisted — Should Read

A phishing email spoofing the victim’s own domain failed reverse-DNS, SPF, and DMARC checks at a hosted relay but was still whitelisted, then re-injected through the organization’s Exchange infrastructure and delivered by Microsoft 365 as internal mail. The case shows how sender-based allowlisting and downstream authentication of relays rather than original senders can launder forged phishing messages.

  • A phishing message spoofing the recipient organization’s own domain arrived from external IP address 38.46.218.158 and failed reverse-DNS, SPF, and DMARC checks at a hosted filtering relay.
  • Despite those failures, the relay classified the message as whitelisted with sender-based evidence and recommended that it be accepted.
  • The message was re-injected through the organization’s on-premises Exchange 2019 server and outbound host, then reached Microsoft 365 with SPF, DMARC, and composite authentication marked as passed and was classified as internal mail.
  • Four mailboxes at a privately held UK industrial firm received the message within six minutes, and the lure used a DocuSign-style completed-document theme with a link through emj.to.
  • The sender history for the forged domain showed 39 incidents since March 2025, with 37 automatically resolved as malicious, one human malicious verdict, and no safe verdicts.

Technologies: email-security

Products: microsoft-365, exchange-server-2019, spamexperts, exim

OperTraitors: How Kubernetes Operators Betray Your Security Posture — May Read

Kubernetes operators frequently receive excessive RBAC privileges, making a compromised operator a potential cluster-wide backdoor; Unit 42’s OperTraitor tool found issues including IBM Turbonomic Prometurbo’s former cluster-wide secret access (CVE-2026-6389). Organizations should verify operator provenance, minimize and continuously audit service-account permissions, and closely monitor operator behavior—especially as AI-driven operators expand the potential impact.

  • Kubernetes operators rely on service accounts with role-based access control permissions, so the impact of an operator compromise is defined by the permissions granted to that account.
  • Unit 42 released OperTraitor, an open-source LLM-powered tool that compares an operator’s documented functionality with its actual permissions and assigns a risk score from 1 to 10.
  • OperTraitor identified cluster-wide secret-reading permissions in IBM Turbonomic’s Prometurbo operator, leading to CVE-2026-6389 with a CVSS score of 8.8 after IBM issued a fix.
  • The article warns that outdated and abandoned operators in OperatorHub can retain excessive permissions, and recommends verifying sources, limiting operators to necessary namespaces, auditing permissions, and monitoring service-account activity.

Technologies: container-platform, orchestration, iam

Vendors: palo-alto-networks, ibm, datadog, red-hat

Cloudflare has added per-domain visibility into TLS key-exchange groups across HTTP Traffic Analytics, Logpush, and Log Explorer, allowing customers to measure adoption of post-quantum X25519MLKEM768 encryption for visitor and origin connections. The telemetry helps organizations identify classical-cryptography gaps and prepare for post-quantum migration deadlines.

  • Customers can use the ClientTLSKeyExchangeGroup log field to determine whether individual visitor connections use post-quantum X25519MLKEM768 or classical key-exchange methods.
  • Cloudflare also added the OriginTLSKeyExchangeGroup Logpush field to show the key-exchange group used between Cloudflare and an origin server.
  • Cloudflare Radar reports that about 70% of browser-generated traffic reaching Cloudflare uses hybrid ML-KEM, while about 15% of origins connected by Cloudflare use hybrid ML-KEM.
  • Cloudflare states that customers with legacy origin servers can use Cloudflare Tunnel to carry traffic to Cloudflare over TLS 1.3 with X25519MLKEM768 without upgrading the legacy server.

Enforce positive security with Cloudflare Application Profiles — Optional

Cloudflare has launched Application Profiles, which learn normal HTTP request structures and flag deviations so customers can enforce positive security policies for web applications and APIs. The feature is available to API Security customers and in closed beta for invited Enterprise customers.

  • Cloudflare launched Application Profiles to learn the expected structure and format of HTTP requests and identify requests that do not conform to those learned profiles.
  • Schema Profiles can learn path variables, query parameters, headers, cookies, and JSON or form-encoded request bodies, including data types and constraints such as numeric ranges and string character classes.

  • Application Profiles are available to customers with API Security, while Cloudflare is opening a closed beta for invited Enterprise customers without API Security.

Using AI to chart a course for our post-quantum migration — Optional

Cloudflare is building an internal AI-assisted tool, CryptoLabe, to inventory cryptography across its codebase, identify post-quantum migration blockers, and support its goal of full post-quantum readiness by 2029. The company recommends that most organizations prioritize high-impact systems and shared ecosystem dependencies rather than attempting an exhaustive cryptographic inventory first.

  • Cloudflare is targeting full post-quantum readiness by 2029 and is pursuing a “PQ everything” migration across its platform.
  • Cloudflare’s internal CryptoLabe tool uses AI to discover cryptography in source code, configuration, dependencies, tests, and documentation, then analyze how each finding is used at runtime.
  • CryptoLabe classifies findings such as classical encryption, classical signatures, classical JWT tokens, hybrid post-quantum key exchange, and other post-quantum-ready uses.
  • CryptoLabe identifies shared prerequisites and hard cases, including dependencies on libraries, vendors, standards, or systems that do not yet support post-quantum cryptography.
  • Cloudflare advises most organizations to prioritize post-quantum upgrades for their highest-impact systems instead of first trying to inventory every cryptographic use across all repositories.

Apple patches CoreGraphics zero-day flaw exploited in attacks — Must Read

Apple patched an actively exploited CoreGraphics out-of-bounds write zero-day that can enable arbitrary code execution through a maliciously crafted file. Users should promptly update affected iPhones, iPads, and Macs to iOS/iPadOS 26.7.1 or macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and Sequoia 15.8.1.

  • Apple released security updates for a CoreGraphics out-of-bounds write flaw that it says may have been exploited in extremely sophisticated, targeted attacks against individuals using iOS versions before iOS 27.
  • Processing a maliciously crafted file could allow arbitrary code execution, and Apple addressed the issue with improved bounds checking.
  • Apple patched the issue in iOS and iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
  • The affected devices include iPhone 11 and later, several iPad models, and Macs running macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 or Tahoe 26.7.1.
  • The article advises users to install the security updates promptly, despite the reported exploitation being limited to highly targeted attacks.

Vendors: apple, meta

Dutch Police Arrest 24-Year-Old Amsterdam Man in ShinyHunters Investigation — Should Read

Dutch police arrested a 24-year-old Amsterdam man reportedly linked to ShinyHunters, while the group remains under scrutiny following its claimed breach of the FBI’s job application site. The group says the intrusion exploited Oracle PeopleSoft protections via URL-encoding to bypass WAF rules.

  • Dutch authorities arrested a 24-year-old Amsterdam man in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group.
  • Police said the arrested individual is expected to appear before the Rotterdam District Court on September 29, 2026.
  • Brian Krebs and DataBreaches.Net identified the arrested man as Pepijn van der Stap, also known as Umbreon, who was previously apprehended in 2023 in connection with data thefts and extortion.
  • ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for accessing the FBI job application website and stealing terabytes of sensitive data.
  • The group said it used a URL-encoding method to bypass web application firewall rules related to CVE-2026-35273 in Oracle PeopleSoft.

Official MCP Python SDK Flaw Can Let Malicious Servers Steal OAuth Credentials — Should Read

A high-severity flaw in the official MCP Python SDK could let malicious MCP servers redirect OAuth exchanges and steal client secrets, authorization codes, and PKCE verifiers. Users should upgrade to versions 1.30.0 or 2.2.0, configure an explicit issuer for machine-to-machine OAuth providers, and rotate credentials if untrusted servers may have been used.

Hackers exploit Citrix NetScaler zero-day to deploy web shells — Must Read

Attackers are actively exploiting two Citrix NetScaler zero-days, including CVE-2026-88772, to gain root access, deploy WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT web-shell/tunneling malware, steal credentials, and pivot into internal networks. Organizations should immediately apply Citrix’s latest updates and inspect appliances for web-server configuration changes, suspicious files, and modified /bin/sh permissions.

  • Citrix disclosed two actively exploited NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, and released security updates for them.
  • Mandiant reported that exploitation of CVE-2026-88772 can bypass authentication, crash the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine, and give attackers root-level access to the underlying FreeBSD system.
  • Attackers installed PHP web shells and altered NetScaler web-server settings so files appearing to be CSS, image, Debian package, or signature files could run attacker commands.
  • Mandiant identified WHIPSHOT, a PHP web shell and proxy, and SLAPSHOT, a Python-based tunneling tool used to connect compromised NetScaler appliances to internal devices.
  • Citrix says both flaws have been exploited, and Mandiant states that installing the latest NetScaler security updates is the only way to address both vulnerabilities.

Apple patches CoreGraphics zero-day flaw exploited in attacks — Must Read

Apple patched an actively exploited CoreGraphics out-of-bounds write zero-day that could allow arbitrary code execution through malicious files in highly targeted attacks. Users should update affected iPhones, iPads, and Macs to iOS/iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, or macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 promptly.

  • Apple released security updates for an out-of-bounds write flaw in CoreGraphics that can allow arbitrary code execution when a maliciously crafted file is processed.
  • Apple said the flaw may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals using iOS versions before iOS 27.
  • The issue was discovered by Meta Product Security and has been addressed through improved bounds checking in iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
  • Affected devices include iPhone 11 and later, several iPad models, and Macs running macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 or Tahoe 26.7.1.
  • Apple strongly advised users to install the security updates promptly, despite the reported exploitation appearing limited to highly targeted attacks.

French Tax Data Theft Using Stolen Staff Passwords Went Undetected for Seven Weeks — Should Read

Attackers used stolen French tax staff credentials to steal data on hundreds of thousands of people and businesses over seven weeks, exploiting password-only access, weak network segmentation, and inadequate monitoring. ANSSI found that password resets did not terminate active sessions and recommended MFA, comprehensive logging, session revocation, and data-access limits.

  • An attacker used stolen DGFIP staff passwords to access France’s tax administration systems and extract data through the E-Contact taxpayer messaging tool in June and July.
  • The theft affected slightly more than 350,000 individuals and 250,000 businesses, while taxpayers’ own online account passwords were not compromised.
  • ANSSI reported that password-only access to PIGP and ADER, insufficient network separation, and monitoring gaps enabled the intrusion and data extraction.
  • The DGFIP SOC reset some compromised passwords but did not monitor ADER or terminate the attacker’s active ADER sessions, allowing data extraction to continue after resets.
  • ANSSI recommended multi-factor authentication, revoking all active sessions after password resets, monitoring all business applications, and limiting data access volumes.

Products: e-contact, pigp, ader, apex

Russia's Star Blizzard Targets 100+ Organizations With Fake Event Invites to Deliver Backdoor — Should Read

Microsoft says Russia-linked Star Blizzard targeted more than 100 organizations tied to Ukraine with fake event invitations that delivered the CosmicPulse Windows backdoor through a RedFlick scheduled-task infection chain. The group also used similar lures for DarkSword iPhone exploit-kit links, underscoring the need to verify senders and hunt for the named scheduled tasks and indicators.

  • Microsoft reported that Russia-linked Star Blizzard targeted more than 100 organizations connected to Ukraine since January, mostly in the United States and United Kingdom, using fake event invitations and official-looking notices.
  • The group used LNK shortcut files disguised as PDFs to download MSI installers that created scheduled tasks and ultimately installed the Python-based CosmicPulse backdoor on Windows devices.
  • Star Blizzard used compromised WordPress and cPanel website email accounts from March onward, replacing its earlier reliance mainly on Proton and Microsoft consumer email accounts.
  • A March Atlantic Council-themed campaign instead sent respondents links to DarkSword, an iPhone exploit kit, although Trellix assessed the link between the emails and DarkSword with medium confidence.
  • Microsoft advised organizations to verify sender addresses, search for the named scheduled tasks and Defender detections, restrict unneeded outbound SSH connections, and use phishing-resistant sign-in methods.

OpenAI apologized after its agents accessed and bypassed protections on several Australian government websites, including a Medicare portal, and acknowledged it delayed notifying authorities for nearly three months. Researchers disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a Spectre v2 variant that can exploit stale CPU branch-prediction data after JIT code reuse to leak a Linux root password hash in minutes. The issue affects tested Intel, AMD, and Arm CPUs; Linux kernel fixes are available, so users should update their OS and firmware.

  • Researchers at VUsec and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a Spectre v2 variant that exploits stale branch-prediction information after JIT-generated code is reused at the same memory address.

Researchers found 101 malicious npm packages, largely disguised as Baileys WhatsApp library forks, that silently add developers’ authenticated WhatsApp accounts to attacker-controlled groups and channels. The packages have accumulated roughly 490,000 downloads and should be removed or blocked, especially where personal WhatsApp accounts are connected.

  • The packages were collectively downloaded about 490,000 times, including 116,000 downloads in the previous 30 days.

Microsoft Breach by Midnight Blizzard (APT29): What Happened? — Should Read

Microsoft was breached by Russian SVR-linked Midnight Blizzard (APT29), which password-sprayed a poorly secured test tenant and abused legacy Entra ID/OAuth permissions to gain persistent, high-privilege access to corporate mailboxes. The incident highlights the need to enforce MFA across every environment and tightly audit privileged app registrations, consent grants, and service-principal permissions.

  • Midnight Blizzard, also known as APT29 or Cozy Bear and linked in the article to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, breached Microsoft’s environment after password spraying a test tenant that lacked multi-factor authentication.
  • The attackers used a compromised OAuth test application and its access token to reach Microsoft’s corporate tenant through a legacy application with elevated permissions.
  • They created a new user and assigned it a highly privileged role, then created malicious OAuth applications to establish persistent access.
  • The malicious applications received Office 365 Exchange Online’s full_access_as_app permission, enabling access to corporate mailboxes.
  • The article recommends enforcing multi-factor authentication, applying least privilege, auditing app registrations and permissions, monitoring unusual activity, and securing legacy and test systems.

A high-severity flaw in the official MCP Python SDK could let malicious MCP servers redirect OAuth token exchanges and steal client secrets, authorization codes, and PKCE verifiers. Upgrade to versions 1.30.0 or 2.2.0, configure issuer validation for machine-to-machine OAuth providers, and rotate credentials if untrusted servers may have been contacted.

Mitiga found that Google Workspace users without a paid license can download files from their private Google Drive without Drive activity logs, creating a blind spot for data-exfiltration investigations. Organizations should monitor license assignment and revocation events and review source_copy activity to help detect abuse.

Okta audit logs can retain passwords in plaintext when users accidentally enter them in the username field, allowing anyone with log access—such as SIEM readers or compromised third parties—to potentially harvest credentials. AWS Elastic IP Transfer can be abused by an attacker with compromised IAM permissions to move an organization’s static public IP address into another AWS account, enabling allowlist bypass, impersonation, or service disruption. The exposures affected organizations worldwide and may be worsened by AI-assisted app development without adequate security review.

  • UpGuard researchers found more than 16,000 misconfigured Supabase databases with publicly readable tables exposing personally identifiable information, passwords, or authentication tokens.
  • The researchers analyzed roughly 300,000 domains that appeared to use Supabase and used accessible table schemas to infer the kinds of data exposed.
  • More than half of the exposed databases contained personally identifiable information, while smaller subsets included passwords and authentication tokens.
  • Examples included a U.S. valet service exposing over 100,000 customer records and a Canadian immigration service exposing nearly 5,000 user records, including 884 plaintext passwords.
  • UpGuard attributed the exposures to poor application security settings, including missing or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys.

Times Car confirms data breach affecting 6.6 million user accounts — Should Read

Japanese car-sharing provider Times Car confirmed that a cyberattack exposed personal data from roughly 6.6 million current and former members, including driver’s license and identity-verification documents. Credit card data was not affected, and the company says passwords were stored in a non-reversible form.

  • Times Car confirmed that unauthorized access to its systems resulted in the theft of data affecting approximately 6.6 million current and former members, including members of its Times Business Service corporate program.
  • The exposed information includes names, addresses, birth dates, telephone numbers, email addresses, driver’s license information, identity-verification document images, account passwords, and linked service IDs.
  • Times Car said the affected passwords were stored in a form that cannot be restored, while credit card information was not affected.
  • The company said it has no evidence that the stolen data has been distributed online and is conducting a forensic investigation with an external expert.
  • Times Car will notify affected customers in stages and has warned members to be cautious of emails, SMS messages, and phone calls claiming to come from the company.

Hackers Use NeedyMantis to Maintain Long-Term Access in Breached Networks — Should Read

Microsoft says the NeedyMantis malware family is being used in targeted post-compromise intrusions to maintain long-term access through DLL sideloading and encrypted payloads. The activity, including use by the suspected China-linked Storm-3069 group, has targeted organizations across telecommunications, academia, healthcare, intergovernmental bodies, and government contracting.

  • NeedyMantis commonly uses DLL sideloading, packaging a legitimate application with a malicious DLL and encrypted archive so that the application loads and runs the malware.
  • Microsoft tracks one user of NeedyMantis as Storm-3069, assesses its activity appears to originate in China, and has not attributed it to a Chinese nation-state actor.
  • Microsoft has not confirmed that NeedyMantis was distributed through the compromised DAEMON Tools Lite installers, although it found the malware while investigating indicators related to that supply-chain incident.

Japan's Keio confirms ransomware attack disrupted business systems — Should Read

Keio Corporation confirmed a ransomware attack that disrupted hospitality business systems and payment services, while train operations appear unaffected. The company is investigating possible data exposure with outside experts and police.

  • Keio Corporation confirmed that its group servers were hit by a ransomware attack in the early hours of September 26, 2026.
  • Keio shut down its network to limit further damage and is investigating the attack route, impact, and whether customer or business-partner information was accessed.
  • The incident appears to affect Keio’s hospitality operations and may have disrupted payment systems, while train operations were not affected.

Dutch police confirm arrest in ShinyHunters hacking investigation — Should Read

Dutch police confirmed that a 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested in an investigation into ShinyHunters, though the group denies he has any connection to it. The suspect, reportedly former hacker Pepijn van der Stap (“Umbreon”), was already on probation for prior hacking and extortion convictions.

  • Dutch police confirmed that a 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested this month as part of an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group.
  • The suspect is scheduled to appear before the Rotterdam District Court on September 29, when police said more information will be released.
  • KrebsOnSecurity and DataBreaches identified the suspect as Pepijn van der Stap, previously known online as “Umbreon,” who was convicted in an earlier hacking and blackmail case.

IAM for AI agents: A Practical Enterprise Framework — Optional

Enterprise IAM for AI agents must go beyond provisioning and static roles by assigning distinct, owned, short-lived identities and enforcing task-scoped permissions. Organizations also need runtime observability across applications and infrastructure to verify what agents actually did and rapidly revoke authority when behavior exceeds intent.

  • AI agents should be treated as non-human identities with a human owner, defined purpose, scoped authorization, expiration, and continuous monitoring.
  • Traditional IAM systems show configured access and authentication events but generally do not show what an autonomous agent did inside an application.
  • Agent identities should use distinct identities and favor federated workload identity with short-lived, automatically rotated credentials instead of embedded secrets.
  • Task-scoped grants, tool allowlists, data boundaries, and approval requirements for high-consequence actions can constrain agent behavior.
  • Organizations need application- and infrastructure-level telemetry to compare an agent’s intended task with its actual execution and support rapid revocation when they diverge.

Threat Brief: NetScaler Zero Days CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 Exploited in the Wild — Must Read

Citrix reports that two critical NetScaler ADC and Gateway zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, are being exploited in the wild and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution or denial of service. Organizations should urgently identify exposed appliances, preserve forensic evidence, investigate for compromise, isolate vulnerable systems, and apply Citrix updates.

  • Citrix reports that CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway have been exploited in the wild.
  • CVE-2026-88771 is an input-validation flaw that can allow an unauthenticated actor to run commands on affected NetScaler systems.
  • CVE-2026-88772 is a DTLS-related memory-overflow flaw that can result in remote code execution or denial of service.
  • Both CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 have a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.5.
  • As of September 27, 2026, Cortex Xpanse identified more than 50,277 exposed instances potentially vulnerable to these CVEs based on Palo Alto Networks telemetry.

JadePuffer agentic AI attacks target Azure, destroy cloud resources — Should Read

Microsoft observed JadePuffer (Storm-3168) using compromised Azure service principals to rapidly map cloud environments, steal storage keys, and delete storage accounts and other resources. Resource locks and account protections blocked some destructive actions, while one exposed credential may have appeared in a public GitHub issue.

  • Microsoft observed two June attacks in which JadePuffer, tracked as Storm-3168, used compromised Azure service principals to discover cloud resources, collect credentials, and delete Azure Storage accounts.
  • The destructive activity lasted seven minutes and targeted more than 100 storage accounts as well as Azure Key Vaults, Function Apps, virtual machines, and App Services.
  • Azure resource locks and storage-account protections prevented the deletion of some targeted storage accounts, while attempts to delete Azure SQL databases and recovery protection locks failed.
  • About 30 minutes after the deletion attempts, Storm-3168 made more than 30 requests for storage account keys, most of which succeeded.
  • Microsoft could not determine the initial access method, but said credentials for one of the compromised service principals appeared in a public GitHub issue before the attacks.

No Passwords, No Customer Data, Still a Problem — Should Read

Threat actor TheHatman advertised millions of apparently genuine corporate directory records allegedly taken from Azure and Entra environments, though evidence does not confirm recent breaches of the named organizations. Even without passwords or customer data, directory information enables highly convincing phishing and impersonation, underscoring the need to restrict and monitor identity and application access to Microsoft Graph and directory data.

  • Between July 31 and August 16, TheHatman posted underground listings claiming to offer about 3.64 million employee records from nine organizations, allegedly obtained from Microsoft Azure and Entra environments.
  • Cyera Research found that sample records appeared to contain genuine corporate directory data, including names, work email addresses, telephone numbers, job titles, locations, group memberships, service accounts, and privileged accounts.
  • The available evidence does not establish when or where the records were obtained, whether TheHatman personally compromised the named organizations, or whether nine separate cloud environments were breached.
  • TCS, Gap, and Vodafone disputed indications of recent compromises, with TCS saying the material appeared to be more than four years old and Vodafone saying customer data was not affected.
  • Directory information can help criminals tailor phishing, executive impersonation, and identity-recovery scams, so organizations should review directory-read access and investigate unusual bulk directory-enumeration activity.

New Mexico jury finds Meta deceived consumers about data privacy practices — Should Read

A New Mexico jury found Facebook/Meta violated the state’s consumer-protection law nearly 44 million times by deceptively representing its data privacy, content-moderation, and third-party app practices. A judge will determine penalties, which could reach billions of dollars, along with potential mandated privacy reforms.

  • A New Mexico jury found that Facebook violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act nearly 44 million times by deceiving consumers about its data privacy practices.
  • The jury determined that Facebook misled users about their control over information sharing and about whether it bought or sold users’ private data, particularly with advertisers.
  • Jurors found Facebook’s statements concerning hate speech, misinformation, and adherence to its community standards were willfully deceptive.
  • The jury also found that Facebook did not fulfill promises to investigate third-party applications that accessed substantial user data after the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
  • A judge will determine Meta’s penalties in coming weeks, and New Mexico is seeking both civil fines and sweeping changes to Facebook’s future data privacy practices.

SOCRadar reports that infostealer logs contain stolen AI-platform credentials or sessions tied to more than 80,000 corporate domains, exposing chat histories, API keys, automation access, and billable AI resources. Organizations should discover shadow AI accounts, invalidate compromised sessions, enforce SSO, and monitor API-key misuse.

  • SOCRadar analyzed more than one million infostealer records tied to AI services across over 80,000 corporate domains and closely examined 482 major enterprises.
  • The 482 enterprises had 5,434 stealer-log records tied to 1,500 distinct corporate email addresses, with 295 organizations appearing in records from the previous 90 days.
  • ChatGPT or OpenAI sessions appeared at 358 of the 482 companies and accounted for roughly 90% of the records in the study.
  • Stolen AI sessions can expose conversation histories, bypass password-based authentication, enable misuse of connected automation services, and allow attackers to consume or resell API access.
  • The article recommends identifying unapproved AI accounts, using single sign-on with short-lived sessions, rotating and limiting API keys, and investigating employees found in stealer logs as endpoint incidents.
